locator: https://digital.csic.es/handle/10261/50304 (PDF, 225.75 kB, viewed in the browser, not downloaded)
how_read: full text read (pages 1 and 3 to 8 of 10, by eye in the browser; the introduction and the reference pages were not read)
quality_note: Peer-reviewed primary study; 49 radio-tracked lynx, 1983 to 1998, Donana (Coto del Rey and Reserva Biologica).  Age at start of dispersal 17.8 +/- 1.2 (SE) months, mostly 13 to 24; by 2 years the probability of having dispersed was at least 0.78 for either sex.  At least 13 of 27 dispersers (48%) settled in a territory; the fate of 7 was unknown.  Annual survival of dispersers 0.480 (12 to 24 months) and 0.442 (24 to 36 months) against 0.915 and 1.000 for lynx that stayed; 8 of 11 deaths of dispersers were illegal hunting.  Dispersal mostly began January to June (22 of 27 in the results; the abstract says 24 of 29).  The probability of dispersal rose with rabbit density in the natal area.  The reference list of palomares2005 gives a different title for the same volume and pages.

quality_note: Primary source of the 1.0 (autumn) and 4.6 (spring) rabbits per hectare figures.  They are the lowest densities recorded, and the study says they were enough to support lynx reproduction; it says it could not determine the minimum density at which lynx fail or the effect of density on how many females breed.  The EU report reads them as needed densities.  Adult female home range 9.5 km2, adult male 18.2, young 7.3; no correlation between rabbit density and range size (P above 0.2).  The printed adult density (0.77 per km2) looks inconsistent with those ranges; the 0.08 per km2 that eu_spain_report2018 cites is its own conversion (not checked).

how_read: full text read (text and tables; the figures are not in the file)
quality_note: Peer-reviewed primary study of radio-tagged lynx in Coto del Rey (Donana), with surveys in 1996 and 1997.  It indexes rabbits by pellet counts and gives one conversion to density:  114 pellets per m2 is about 4.6 rabbits per hectare in spring and 1.0 in autumn (citing Palomares, in press, which its reference list gives as the Wildlife Society Bulletin paper on three ways to estimate rabbit abundance; we read that paper on 2026-10-25 as palomares2001b and found no such conversion in it, so the conversion's origin is unverified).  Resident range size fell as pellets rose, but across only five ranges, with one female range inferred from male ranges, a strongly correlated second predictor (short shrub cover, r = -0.98), and one influential point; treat it as weak evidence on range size.  Resident sites averaged 79.7 pellets per m2 in autumn, against 31.6 at unused sites and 35.3 at dispersal sites.

citation: Palomares F (2001).  Comparison of 3 methods to estimate rabbit abundance in a Mediterranean environment.  Wildlife Society Bulletin 29(2): 578-585 (the repository record says 578-582; the printed page footers say 578-585).
locator: https://digital.csic.es/handle/10261/51227 (PDF, 1.01 MB, viewed in the browser, not downloaded)
how_read: full text read (scanned PDF, read by eye in the browser)
quality_note: Peer-reviewed primary study in Coto del Rey, June 1994 to August 1995, in 6 habitats: line transects, pellet counts, and warren counts.  Rabbit density (line transect) in Mediterranean scrubland was 13.2 to 41.5 per hectare across the year, and on average 4.1 times lower in October than in April to June.  Pellet counts predicted density poorly in scrubland (adjusted r2 0.10, P = 0.082, n = 23) and better when edge plots replaced scrubland plots (adjusted r2 0.43, P < 0.001); the author concludes that uncontrolled pellet counts cannot estimate abundance accurately but may give an acceptable approximation of relative abundance.

quality_note: Peer-reviewed primary study; 17 adult resident females in two Donana subpopulations, 1985 to 2008, 6 of them given supplementary food.
